reference.source: Scriver's OMMBID / Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics
clinicalPearls: A rare inborn error of serine and fructose metabolism caused by deficiency of D-glycerate kinase (GLYCTK)
The clinical spectrum is broad and variable, ranging from severe encephalopathy with seizures and developmental delay to essentially asymptomatic individuals
Reported features in symptomatic cases include hypotonia, microcephaly, seizures, metabolic acidosis and failure to thrive
The biochemical marker is markedly increased urinary D-glyceric acid on organic acid analysis
The variable phenotype means the metabolite finding does not reliably predict clinical severity
Management is supportive; no specific corrective therapy is established, and dietary measures are individualised through a metabolic service
Diagnosis rests on urine organic acids with confirmatory GLYCTK molecular testing
reference.pathophysiology: D-glycerate kinase phosphorylates D-glycerate to 2-phosphoglycerate, linking the metabolism of serine and fructose to glycolytic intermediates. Enzyme deficiency causes accumulation and urinary excretion of D-glyceric acid. The mechanism by which the metabolite relates to the neurological features is not fully defined, and because some individuals with the biochemical defect remain well, the accumulated acid may not be directly and uniformly neurotoxic. The disorder is therefore biochemically defined but clinically heterogeneous.
additionalDifferentials: Other organic acidaemias presenting with encephalopathy
L-glyceric aciduria (primary hyperoxaluria type 2), a biochemically distinct disorder
Other causes of infantile epileptic encephalopathy
Non-metabolic causes of developmental delay and hypotonia
additionalInvestigations: Urine organic acids demonstrating increased D-glyceric acid
Blood gas and lactate to assess metabolic acidosis
Exclusion of other organic acidaemias on the same organic acid profile
redFlags: Failure to thrive with progressive neurological signs
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is highly variable: some patients have severe neurological impairment while others are asymptomatic, so counselling must reflect this heterogeneity rather than the biochemical finding alone.
pitfalls: Confusing D-glyceric aciduria with L-glyceric aciduria (primary hyperoxaluria type 2)
Assuming the metabolite level predicts clinical severity
Over-treating an incidentally detected, asymptomatic biochemical abnormality
Attributing all neurological findings to the disorder without excluding co-existing causes
references: Scriver's OMMBID, disorders of organic acid metabolism
Nelson Textbook of Paediatrics, organic acid disorders
management: Manage through a metabolic medicine service with supportive, symptom-directed care, as no specific corrective therapy is established
Individualise dietary measures, including consideration of fructose intake, under specialist metabolic dietetic supervision
Correct metabolic acidosis and provide fluid and buffering support during acute decompensation
Treat seizures with antiepileptic drugs where epilepsy is present
Provide developmental support and monitor growth for failure to thrive
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal recessive GLYCTK disorder, stressing the wide phenotypic variability so that counselling is not based on the biochemical finding alone
